items.prompt: What is the main idea?
options: The main way to improve public rest space is to maximize the number of seats
A bench’s usefulness depends on its context and actual users
The intended purpose of seating should take priority over how people actually use it
The same bench design creates the same behavior everywhere
items.explanation: Location, access and observed use determine usefulness.
items.title: The social life of a public bench
items.passage:
A bench appears to be a simple facility: it provides a place to sit. Its position, however, can influence who uses a public space and how they use it. A bench beside a busy path offers opportunities to observe passing activity. One facing a quieter garden may attract people seeking a break from that activity. The same design can serve different purposes depending on where it is placed.
Small practical details also matter. Shade may make a seat useful during hot hours, while a nearby path allows people with limited mobility to reach it. If planners count only the total number of benches, they can overlook these differences in access and comfort. Ten poorly located seats do not necessarily provide more usable rest space than a smaller number placed with care.
Observation is useful because intended and actual use may differ. A seating area planned for conversation might instead become a popular place to wait for a bus. This does not automatically indicate failure; it may reveal a need that planners had not recognized. The appropriate response could be to support that use rather than prevent it.
Public furniture therefore participates in the organization of everyday life. Evaluating it requires attention to people’s activities and the surrounding environment, not merely an inventory of objects.

items.prompt: Why can unfinished objects be informative?
options: They retain traces hidden by later finishing
Their visible surfaces record later alterations more clearly than early shaping
Their marks show the standard sequence normally followed by the maker
They eliminate the need to study tools and waste
items.explanation: Early shaping marks can remain visible.
items.title: Evidence preserved by an unfinished object
items.passage:
Museums often display completed objects, but unfinished work can offer unusually clear evidence of a craft process. A finished stone carving may hide the marks of early shaping beneath a smooth surface. An abandoned piece can preserve several stages at once, allowing researchers to see where rough material was removed and where finer work had begun.
Interpreting such an object still requires caution. A partly completed feature does not necessarily show the normal order of work. The maker might have been experimenting, responding to damaged material, or following a particular customer’s request. Several unfinished examples are more informative than one because repeated patterns can be distinguished from unusual decisions.
Tools and waste material provide additional clues. A tool mark on the object may correspond to a particular cutting edge, while discarded fragments can suggest how the original block was divided. When these sources agree, a reconstruction of the process becomes more convincing. When they do not, the disagreement identifies a question for further investigation.
An unfinished object is thus not merely an imperfect version of a completed one. It can be evidence of actions that the finished surface no longer displays. Its value lies partly in what was left visible when production stopped.

items.prompt: What problem with same-type practice is identified?
options: It makes later assessments contain fewer problem types
It prevents learners from becoming faster at any procedure
It may hide difficulty choosing an appropriate method
It requires students to invent a new method for every question
items.explanation: A predictable sequence removes the need to select among methods.
items.title: Why mixing practice problems can help
items.passage:
A student who completes several problems of the same kind may become quick at applying a familiar procedure. This fluency can create an impression of strong understanding. On a later assessment, however, the student may struggle when different kinds of problems appear together and the appropriate procedure is no longer obvious.
Mixing problem types during practice can address this difficulty. In addition to carrying out a method, the learner must decide which method fits each problem. That decision requires attention to the structure of the problem rather than to its position in a sequence. For example, a student cannot assume that the next question calls for the same calculation as the previous one.
Mixed practice can feel slower and less successful at first. Frequent mistakes do not automatically mean that it is ineffective; they may reveal decisions that repeated same-type practice allowed the learner to avoid. Nevertheless, some initial familiarity with the individual methods is useful. A learner who has never encountered any of them may be occupied entirely with basic steps.
The distinction is between practice that makes performance easy now and practice that supports choosing and applying knowledge later. A useful study plan can include both concentrated work on a method and opportunities to distinguish it from alternatives.

items.prompt: What is the purpose of a canal lock?
options: To keep every canal at a single height
To move boats between water levels
To prevent water entering a closed chamber

items.explanation: A lock connects stretches at different heights.
items.title: How a canal lock changes a boat’s level

stimulus.title: How a canal lock changes a boat’s level
stimulus.script:
A canal may need to carry boats between stretches of water at different heights. A lock provides a way to make that change in a controlled chamber. Gates separate the chamber from the higher and lower stretches, and openings allow water to enter or leave.
Imagine a boat entering from the lower side. After the lower gates close, water is admitted from the higher side. As the water level in the chamber rises, the floating boat rises with it. When the level matches the upper stretch, the upper gates can open and the boat can continue. Going down reverses the process: water leaves the closed chamber until its level matches the lower stretch.
The gates are not simply doors that can be opened whenever a boat is ready. A difference in water level creates pressure, so the levels on either side need to be suitably matched. The sequence of closing, filling or emptying, and opening is part of what makes the passage possible.
A lock is a useful example of working with a physical process rather than lifting the boat directly with a machine. The boat remains supported by water throughout the change. Understanding that support helps explain why the chamber’s water level, not the boat’s position alone, determines the sequence of operations.

options: A platform pushed upward from beneath it

The opening of both sets of gates at once
The rising water on which it floats
items.explanation: The boat rises with the water admitted to the chamber.

items.prompt: Why should costumes be tested under stage lights?
options: Their appearance can change with the light falling on them

items.explanation: The lighting changes the reflected appearance.
items.title: Lighting a stage with color

stimulus.title: Lighting a stage with color
stimulus.script:
Stage lighting does more than make performers visible. It also affects how scenery and costumes appear. A surface looks a particular color partly because of the light it reflects. Change the light falling on it, and its appearance may change even though the material itself is unchanged.
This is why a costume selected under ordinary room lighting should be tested on the stage. A fabric that seems distinct from the background in the workroom may become difficult to distinguish under the performance lights. Conversely, a small difference that looked unimportant earlier may become very noticeable.
Designers therefore test combinations rather than choosing every element separately. Lighting, scenery, and costume teams need to see how their decisions interact. A photograph of one item under different lighting may not be enough, particularly if the camera adjusts the image automatically.
The goal isn’t always to make the colors look natural. An unusual change may help establish a mood or signal a transition. But it should be a deliberate effect rather than a surprise discovered during the performance. What matters is control over the relationship between light and materials. The example shows why a successful design often depends on checking components together in the conditions in which people will actually experience them.

items.prompt: What distinction does the talk make?
options: Using landmarks versus recognizing any familiar place
Remembering a destination versus knowing its name

items.title: Following a familiar route

stimulus.title: Following a familiar route
stimulus.script:
Think about a route you travel often. At first, you may need to remember a sequence of instructions: turn at the bank, cross a street, then find a particular entrance. With experience, some decisions become easier. Familiar landmarks allow you to recognize where you are without consciously repeating every instruction.
This efficiency has a limit. If the usual entrance closes, knowing the familiar sequence may not be enough to choose an alternative. Someone who understands how the streets connect can take a different path, while someone relying only on a chain of remembered turns may need new directions.
The two kinds of knowledge aren’t necessarily separate achievements acquired once and for all. Exploring a neighborhood, looking at a map, and using different routes can gradually connect familiar landmarks into a wider understanding of the area. A person may know one district in that way while still following a rigid sequence somewhere else.
So successful navigation is not simply a matter of memorizing more instructions. It can also involve learning relationships that allow those instructions to be changed. A disruption that seems inconvenient may expose the difference: can we only repeat the usual route, or can we explain why another route should reach the same destination?

items.explanation: A disruption tests flexibility beyond the learned sequence.

With experience, some decisions become easier. Familiar landmarks allow you to recognize where you are without consciously repeating every instruction.
This efficiency has a limit. If the usual entrance closes, knowing the familiar sequence may not be enough to choose an alternative. Someone who understands how the streets connect can take a different path, while someone relying only on a chain of remembered turns may need new directions.
The two kinds of knowledge aren’t necessarily separate achievements acquired once and for all. Exploring a neighborhood, looking at a map, and using different routes can gradually connect familiar landmarks into a wider understanding of the area. A person may know one district in that way while still following a rigid sequence somewhere else.
So successful navigation is not simply a matter of memorizing more instructions. It can also involve learning relationships that allow those instructions to be changed. A disruption that seems inconvenient may expose the difference: can we only repeat the usual route, or can we explain why another route should reach the same destination?

items.prompt: Why does the speaker ask about reaching the same destination by another route?
options: To recommend that travelers avoid their normal destination
To highlight the flexibility that connected knowledge provides
To suggest that every disruption requires a new map
To explain why memorizing routes is never useful
items.explanation: The final question focuses on using relationships to adapt.

items.title: Write for an Academic Discussion
items.question: People increasingly rely on short summaries to keep up with information. Should schools encourage students to use summaries as a regular study tool, or should they place greater emphasis on reading complete source materials? Explain your view and how it would affect students’ learning.
students: Summaries are useful because students face more material than they can read in full. A well-written overview helps them identify important ideas and decide which sources deserve closer attention. That is a valuable skill in itself.

Complete sources should have priority. A summary may leave out the reasoning or uncertainty behind a conclusion. Students can repeat the main point without understanding why it is supported or where it might not apply.
